record.abstract:
<jats:title>One program to rule them all</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Computers can beat humans at increasingly complex games, including chess and Go. However, these programs are typically constructed for a particular game, exploiting its properties, such as the symmetries of the board on which it is played. Silver
                    <jats:italic>et al.</jats:italic>
                    developed a program called AlphaZero, which taught itself to play Go, chess, and shogi (a Japanese version of chess) (see the Editorial, and the Perspective by Campbell). AlphaZero managed to beat state-of-the-art programs specializing in these three games. The ability of AlphaZero to adapt to various game rules is a notable step toward achieving a general game-playing system.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Science</jats:italic>
                    , this issue p.
                    <jats:related-article xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="doi" issue="6419" page="1140" related-article-type="in-this-issue" vol="362" xlink:href="10.1126/science.aar6404">1140</jats:related-article>
                    ; see also pp.
                    <jats:related-article xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="doi" issue="6419" page="1087" related-article-type="in-this-issue" vol="362" xlink:href="10.1126/science.aaw2221">1087</jats:related-article>
                    and
                    <jats:related-article xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="doi" issue="6419" page="1118" related-article-type="in-this-issue" vol="362" xlink:href="10.1126/science.aav1175">1118</jats:related-article>
                  </jats:p>
title: A general reinforcement learning algorithm that masters chess, shogi, and Go through self-play
